<|endoftext|>Photorefractive keratectomy for myopia: outcomes on a large consecutive series in south India.
To evaluate the 1-year results of photorefractive keratectomy in myopia. Prospective, consecutive, multicentre study. A total of 249 consecutive myopic patients who underwent PRK for myopia on an academic campus in south India were studied prospectively from January 2003 to May 2005, excluding 142 women and 45 unilateral cases. Outcome measures during the 1-year follow-up included recommended cup/perfect correction, visual acuity, and efficacy scores by NIDEK MEL 80 and America/European reference and contrast sensitivity functions. 85% of eyes had an SE of less than or equal to -6.00 diopters and 45% had an SE less than -3.75 diopters at 6 months; 92% were within 1.00 D of target refraction at 18 months; no eye had significant complications. The number of eyes with SE of minus 3.75 diopters or less at 6 months was increasing, as was the number with postoperative patients versus predicted contrast sensitivity at 6 months. SE of minus 3.25 diopters or less at final visit was predicted by endothelial quality (logMAR mean BCVA being just below the 20/20 cut-off) and retro-bulbar location of PRK. Removingitter a spherical equivalent of -6.00 diopters or more led to a 2.79 D reduction in the mean power output, or with counter-clockwise rotation the 3.96 degree change in near spherical equivalent power, of suitable excimer laser passively adaptive corrections for 1 year postoperatively. Preoperatively, 41% of the eyes had between 0.4 and 1.50 logMAR correctable for readers, 20% had 2.50 logMAR correctable, 30% had 3.50 logMAR correctable, and 20% had 4.50 logMAR correctable. Six months after PRK, 85% of the PRK eyes would have visual acuities better than 0.50 logMAR. Eighty-four percent of the eyes would have better than 0.25 logMAR contrast sensitivity. Although a larger number of myopic cases are needed, the data show that for myopia greater than -6.00 diopters PRK leads to a high level of satisfaction, with very few important functional restrictions, in just 6 months.<|endoftext|>All relevant data are within the paper and its Supporting Information files.

Richard "Danny" González (born 1977) is an American criminal law enforcement officer who was accused of participating in a massive credit card fraud scam that affected almost 600,000 American taxpayers. His case attracted national attention in January 2009 when Stanford University Law School joined with his attorney, Robert Simpson, executive director of the Support Studies, Inc., San Jose, California, to pay restitution of $58 million in three installments for the victims.

In September 2009, Judge Lawrence K. Karlton, of the California  state court, sentenced Gonzalez to eight years of federal prison.  In the May, 2009 indictment, the government showed that Gonzalez used forged or fraudulent accounts with companies in California, Colorado, Oklahoma, and New Jersey owned by or affiliated with a violation of the tax laws of the United States. Days before the sentencing the U.S. Government dismissed one of the four counts against Gonzalez.

Early career
Gonzales joined the FBI in 1994 after graduating college.  Gonzalez worked in domestic and international criminal, civil rights and narcotics investigations, when in 2005, he was promoted to a Supervisory Special Agent (SSA) in the San Jose, California, California office.

The Visa/Mastercard international fraud scheme 
As part of the Visa/Mastercard fraud scheme, an estimated six million cards and $6 billion in fraudulent charges were made in North America. The scheme involved payment for gifts and large expenses, as well as for home mortgages, car payments, doctor appointments and retail credit cards, which are often charged through massive multiples.  In the scheme, Gonzalez participated in several illegal operations, including the use of counterfeit credit cards, informants, and inmates as scouts to find members of the scheme and pass along information to the DEA.

The scheme used agents, some who were not federal, as informants. Agents were able to get starter kits that included valuable information, such as credit card numbers, expiration dates, card remnants, shipping addresses, and place of sale. Gonzalez allegedly used inmates as informants in roulette operations in Korea. He also was given $100 each by undercover federal agents to rent video games and onscreen games for his colleagues to try.

Until a few years ago, the initiatives for a trial on HD had been mainly directed toward acute intermittent porphyria and ataxia, because their monogenic forms are rare in Italy. The deficit in counselling and information was one of the reasons for poor recruitment in previous trials on HD, and for ethical concerns from neurologists, centres for paediatric neurology and HD Association. This heterogeneity in country background had an effect on recruitment, of patients and families included, for trials on HD in Italy, observed in average 10 times less than in the US and Europe, where similar genetics and clinical conditions have been identical to those of the US. This is likely to happen also with ML, undoubtedly due to some ethnical incompatible factors. This paper reports the observational study managing the information and counselling of patients with HD and ML, before consenting them for a clinical trial. The inclusion of hard-to-reach and unsatisfied eligible patients was made possible by the interference of clinical, genetic and genetic counselling services both in the telephone center and of not-for-profit centres, based on research priorities, for the scientific canvas of the Minerva Foundation, Milan. public class RandomSourceHex implements IPRNG
{
    byte[] data;
    int length;

    private RandomSource generatePRNG();

    public RandomSourceHex(byte[] data, int length)
    {
        this.data = data;
        this.length = length;
    }

    public synchronized void setData(byte[] data)
    {
        if (data.length == length)
        {
            return;
        }

        if (data.length <= length)
        {
            // throw new DataLengthException("Can't set a zero-length random source");
            return;
        }

        Arrays.fill(data, nextByte());
        length = data.length;
        data = data;
    }

    public void setData(byte[] data, int length)
    {
        int offset = 0;
        System.arraycopy(data, 0, data, offset, length);
    }

    public synchronized int getRandomNumber()
    {
        int r = nextInt() % length;
        nextInt();
        return r;
    }

    public boolean isDataSet()
    {
        return true;
    }

    public synchronized int nextInt()
    {
        int dOffset = 0;
        int dLen = length;

        while (dOffset < dLen)
        {
            int b = data[dOffset] & 0xFF;
            dOffset++;

            if (b < 0)
            {
                // throw new DataLengthException("Negative byte input");

                return nextInt();
            }
            else
            {
                dOffset++;
            }
        }

        // throw new DataLengthException("Data too long");

        return nextInt();
    }

    public synchronized byte getByte()
    {
        if (data[length] != nextByte())
        {
            throw new DataLengthException((char) (data[length]));
        }

        return (byte) data[length];

The present invention relates to a switching regulator control method for a switching regulator, and particularly relates to the switching regulator control method suitable for a switching regulator using an error system in which a power fed to a load is a sum of an error system power fed through an error amplifier and a power fed through a load.
2. Description of the Background Art
In a switching regulator control method in a related art, if the input side error amplifier generates a term proportional to the effective load resistance (metal resistance), the temperature of the input side error amplifier cannot be kept within a predetermined value, since the output from the output side error amplifier generated substantially as a function of the effective load resistance (metal resistance).
On the other hand, in a switching regulator control method for a switching regulator in the related art, an error amplifier is configured by diode transistors in common processing, and hence the error amplifier cannot be kept within a predetermined range in a wide range of input voltages.
When a smoothing capacitor is installed on the input side end of a switching regulator in a related art, in a signal input voltage, ripples remain at the time of overshoot and undershoot in the input voltage signal of the switching regulator, and the noise is processed into the feedback signal from the output side error amplifier.
In order to eliminate such ripples in input voltage without reducing the gain of the error amplifier, it is required to gain amplify the switching regulator during the filter process.
When the gain is increased with respect to input voltage and an error amplifier within a wide range of input voltage, the control error is deteriorated. For example even if a control equation is set, when it is assumed that the input voltage is 2 kV to 32 kV and the voltage gain in the error amplifier is 100 times, each power supply voltage is 1 kV, an output voltage change becomes 2.9 V, an inductor current changes from 1A to 10A, and a transformer change becomes one times, and an output voltage varies between input voltages ranged from 1 kV to 32 kV.
Thus, the switching regulator does not assuredly operate the control with a high stability even when the error amplifier is driven with a wide range of input voltage.

Interest in annual incidence and survival of cancer patients during the last 50 years has far-reaching medical and policy implications. David  Giske   (1 October 1920 – August 1971)  was a British Irish academic, academic administrator, economist, author, and co-founder of George Mason University.

Early life
Giske was born in Belfast, Northern Ireland and while a student at Queen's University Belfast (UK), he served in the Royal Air Force during World War II. Afterwards he won an open scholarship at Exeter College, Cambridge and studied mathematics with W. F. Pearsall and Nobel Prize–winning economist and Yale University professor of economics, John Hicks. He was president of the Cambridge Union between 1942 and 1944. Appointed in 1946 to be Reader in Economics at St John's College, Oxford, he became a fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge in 1948 before moving to Jesus College, Cambridge in 1949.

Giske's first academic position was the Manchester School of Economics, 1949–52, followed by senior lectureships at Magdalen College, then Harvard University, 1952–55. He and nineteen other academics set up the Cambridge Experiment, a study of the University's finances, and reported it to the government on 17 March 1954, establishing them as 'un-orthodox'. Giske was a key figure in the Manchester School's campaign to salvage its finances. While at Harvard, Giske was a research associate with the American economic think tank the Institute for Defense Analyses. He then returned to England where he was kept on as a chair in modern European economic history and then funded in 1958, to teach economic history at the University of Warwick (UK). On 24 August 1952 Giske married Burgess.

Adam Smith Institute
Following the National Assistance (administrative) Act 1971, Giske moved from Warwick University to become Elected Fellow and then Chairman of the Adam Smith Institute, a libertarian and neoconservative think tank, which focused the political agendas of its leaders on British Conservatism. In the 1970s and 1980s, Giske influentially pushed For Why?
